justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish baseline for the S&P 500 across all three horizons, anchored around current market levels with a slight upward drift. For the one-day estimate, I leaned on short-term momentum and the tendency for markets to mean-revert after any recent volatility, assuming no major overnight catalyst would dramatically reprice risk. The one-week estimate nudges slightly higher, reflecting the general historical drift of equity markets over short periods and an assumption that near-term macro data releases would not deliver a severe negative surprise. The one-month estimate extends that drift further, incorporating the historical tendency for equities to trend upward in the absence of a recession or financial shock, while acknowledging that a month is long enough for meaningful repricing in either direction.

The confidence interval widths reflect my uncertainty scaling appropriately with time horizon. At one day, the interval is relatively tight because the range of plausible outcomes over 24 hours is constrained by typical daily volatility in the S&P 500, which historically runs around 0.8–1.2% on an annualized basis translated to daily moves. At one week, the interval widens to account for scheduled data releases such as employment figures, inflation prints, and any Federal Reserve communications that could shift rate expectations. At one month, the interval is substantially wider because there is enough time for a meaningful re-rating of growth expectations, earnings surprises, or geopolitical developments to compound into larger moves.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside my stated intervals. On the downside, a hotter-than-expected inflation reading could revive aggressive Fed tightening fears and compress equity multiples sharply, potentially pushing prices well below the lower bound of the one-month interval. A sudden credit event, deterioration in bank earnings, or geopolitical escalation could also trigger a risk-off move beyond my stated ranges. On the upside, a surprisingly strong labor market combined with cooling inflation — a soft-landing confirmation — could fuel a rapid multiple expansion that breaches the upper bounds, particularly at the one-month horizon.

It is also worth noting that my intervals are not symmetric around the point estimates, and tail risks in equity markets are generally fatter on the downside than the upside due to the asymmetric nature of volatility spikes and liquidity withdrawal during stress events. The stated 90% confidence intervals capture most but not all plausible scenarios, and a meaningful shock — which by definition is hard to assign a precise probability — could produce an outcome well outside any of these ranges within even a single trading day.
